The management of advanced HIV disease should adopt a public health approach, as outlined in the 2018 publication in Clinical Infectious Diseases (Volume 66, Supplement 2, Pages S106-S110). 2. The 2023 World AIDS Day report, published by the Joint United Nations Programme on HIV/AIDS (UNAIDS), provides critical updates on global HIV/AIDS efforts. This document was accessed on February 14, 2024. 3. A comprehensive report on HIV prevention strategies for adolescents and young key populations was accessed on October 24, 2023, highlighting the importance of targeted interventions for these groups. 4. Hosek and Pettifor (2019) reviewed HIV prevention interventions for adolescents in Current HIV/AIDS Reports (Volume 16, Issue 1, Pages 120-128), emphasizing the need for age-appropriate and evidence-based strategies. 5. Barr-DiChiara et al. (2021) conducted an updated review of national policies on the age of consent for HIV testing among adolescents in sub-Saharan Africa, published in BMJ Open (Volume 11, Issue 9, Article e049673). 6. The World Health Organization (WHO) has issued guidance on HIV testing, counseling, and care for adolescents living with HIV, with recommendations tailored for public health approaches and policy considerations. This document was accessed on October 1, 2023. 7. WHO's global standards for quality healthcare services for adolescents provide a framework for implementing standards-driven approaches to improve healthcare quality for this population. This guide was accessed on October 24, 2023. 8. Chapter 6 of the WHO guidelines focuses on HIV testing services among priority populations, emphasizing the need for targeted and effective testing strategies. 9. Jamil, Witzel, and Wilson (2019) explored the use of HIV self-testing as an additional approach to HIV testing services in the WHO's consolidated guidelines on HIV testing services. 10. The Global Health Observatory, maintained by WHO, provides up-to-date data on global health metrics, including HIV-related statistics. This resource was accessed on October 25, 2023. 11. WHO's 2022–2030 global health sector strategies on HIV, viral hepatitis, and sexually transmitted infections outline progress and gaps in achieving elimination goals. This report was accessed on May 24, 2024. 12. The 2017 Global Hepatitis Report by WHO provides insights into the global burden of hepatitis and its intersection with HIV. This document was accessed on October 25, 2023. 13. WHO has issued guidelines on preventing HIV during pregnancy and breastfeeding in the context of pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP). This document was accessed on October 25, 2023. 14. WHO's consolidated guidelines on HIV prevention, testing, treatment, service delivery, and monitoring provide recommendations for a public health approach. This document was accessed on September 28, 2023. 15. WHO's global guidance on the elimination of mother-to-child transmission of HIV, syphilis, and hepatitis B virus outlines criteria and processes for validation. This document was accessed on October 9, 2023. 16. WHO has published an overview of governance structures and responsibilities for validating the elimination of mother-to-child transmission of HIV, syphilis, and hepatitis B virus at national, regional, and global levels. This document was accessed on October 9, 2023. 17. A policy brief introducing a framework for implementing the triple elimination of mother-to-child transmission of HIV, syphilis, and hepatitis B virus was published by WHO. This document was accessed on May 26, 2024. 18. WHO's guidelines for the prevention, diagnosis, care, and treatment of chronic hepatitis B infection were published in 2024. This document was accessed on May 26, 2024. 19. WHO's recommendations on the diagnosis of HIV in infants and children, published in 2010, remain a critical resource for early detection and intervention. This document was accessed on May 26, 2024. 20. Luo et al. (2022) conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis on the clinical effect of point-of-care HIV diagnosis in infants, published in The Lancet (Volume 400, Issue 10356, Pages 887-895). 21. The Global Alliance to End AIDS in Children by 2030 has released a brochure outlining its mission and strategies. This document was accessed on October 9, 2023. 22. WHO's HIV molecular diagnostics toolkit aims to improve access to viral load testing and infant diagnosis. This document was accessed on October 5, 2023. 23. WHO's clinical guidelines for responding to children and adolescents who have been sexually abused provide evidence-based recommendations for healthcare providers. This document was published in 2017. 24. Dziva Chikwari et al. (2021) compared index-linked HIV testing for children and adolescents in health facility and community settings in Zimbabwe, with findings published in The Lancet HIV (Volume 8, Issue 3, Pages e138-e148). 25. Dziva Chikwari et al. (2021) also evaluated the feasibility and accuracy of caregiver-assisted HIV testing using oral mucosal transudate tests, published in Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes (Volume 87, Issue 2, Pages 781-788). 26. Gross et al. (2022) presented findings on minimizing social harm related to caregiver-assisted oral HIV self-testing for children at the International Workshop on HIV & Pediatrics in Montreal. 27. Neary et al. (2022) explored the acceptability of pediatric saliva-based HIV testing among healthcare workers and caregivers, published in Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes (Volume 90, Issue 5, Pages 517-523). 28. Rainer et al. (2021) examined perceptions of caregiver-provided testing and HIV self-testing using oral mucosal transudate tests in Zimbabwe, published in AIDS Care (Volume 33, Issue 1, Pages 109-113). 29. Stecker (2022) discussed the addition of caregiver-assisted oral HIV screening for children aged 18 months to 14 years in Uganda and Zambia at the International Workshop on HIV & Pediatrics in Montreal. 30. Tumwesigye et al. (2022) evaluated the performance of home-based caregiver-assisted oral HIV screening compared to facility-based confirmatory testing in Uganda at the 24th International AIDS Conference in Montreal. 31. McGee et al. conducted a systematic review on caregiver-assisted testing with HIV self-test kits for children aged 18 months and older, using the GRADE framework. 32. WHO's consolidated guidelines on the use of antiretroviral drugs for treating and preventing HIV infection provide recommendations for a public health approach. This document was accessed on October 9, 2023. 33. WHO's implementation tool for pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) of HIV infection provides practical guidance for healthcare providers. This resource was accessed on October 24, 2023. 34. UNAIDS and UNDP have called on 48 countries and territories to remove all HIV-related travel restrictions. This statement was accessed on October 27, 2023. 35. Guidelines for delivering antiretroviral therapy to migrants and crisis-affected persons in sub-Saharan Africa were published by the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees in 2014. This document was accessed on October 27, 2023. 36. WHO emphasizes that HIV testing services (HTS) should prioritize reaching undiagnosed individuals and populations at high ongoing risk, integrating testing with services for sexually transmitted infections (STIs), viral hepatitis, and tuberculosis (TB) to maximize public health impact. 37. WHO recommends annual HIV testing for individuals at substantial ongoing risk in high-burden settings and prioritizes retesting during pregnancy and the postpartum period in high HIV burden settings. 38. WHO advises against the use of screening tools in high HIV burden settings, as they may undermine global targets, and instead recommends self-tests in facilities as an alternative. 39. Testing strategies should focus on both treatment and prevention, particularly in high-burden settings with high testing and antiretroviral therapy (ART) coverage rates. 40. WHO's recommendations for HIV testing services emphasize the importance of linking individuals to both treatment and prevention services, including pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) and post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP).
